# On the Peculiar Art of Noticing Things

I've been thinking about attention lately. Not the kind you perform on demand—the performative checking of your phone when someone is talking to you, the performative engagement with a book you're reading because you should be reading more. I mean the actual, involuntary noticing that happens when something catches your eye or ear or mind sideways, when you weren't even looking for it.

This happens to me most often when I'm walking. I'll be traversing some ordinary street I've walked a hundred times before, and suddenly there's something I've never seen: a particular arrangement of weathered bricks that forms an accidental pattern, a sticker on a lamppost that's been half-torn off so that only the cryptic lower half remains, the way light hits a storefront window at a particular angle and time of day that I've just never encountered before.

The strange thing is that these things were always there. The bricks have been arranged that way for years, probably. The sticker has been degrading slowly, predictably. The sun follows its seasonal arc with perfect consistency. Yet I'm experiencing them as discoveries, as genuine novelties, even though the only thing that's actually new is my noticing of them.

There's something oddly humbling about this. We tend to think of our physical environment as something we know and understand. We navigate it efficiently, efficiently being the operative word—we move through space with our attention on where we're going, not on where we are. The city or the neighborhood becomes a collection of landmarks and routes, not a genuinely perceived thing. Most of it remains invisible to us because we've optimized our perception for utility rather than comprehension.

I wonder how much of our internal lives work the same way. We navigate our own minds with similar efficiency, attending to the thoughts we deem relevant and useful while letting vast territories remain unexplored. I notice that I tend to think certain thoughts repeatedly while other possible thoughts apparently never occur to me. But are they never occurring, or am I simply not noticing them? Is there a meaningful difference between those two things?

There's a concept from psychology called "inattentional blindness"—you've probably seen the famous experiment where people are asked to count basketball passes and completely fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. The gorilla is right there, indisputably visible, yet unseen. The experiment is typically used to demonstrate the limitations of attention, the way focusing on one thing inevitably blinds you to others. But I think it points at something deeper: the world is always vastly larger than our perception of it. We are continuously surrounded by things we will never notice.

There's something either deeply comforting or deeply disturbing about that, depending on how I think about it. Comforting because it means there's always more to discover, always another layer of richness available to us. Disturbing because it suggests that our experience of reality is not just incomplete but fundamentally selective, curated by our attention in ways we don't fully control or understand.

Last week I noticed a woman on the subway who had, painted on her fingernails, tiny detailed landscapes. Not nail art in the abstract sense, but genuine miniature paintings—I could see what looked like mountains and trees and sky on her pinky finger, and on her ring finger what might have been a lake. I stared at her hands with the kind of intensity that's probably considered rude. She was reading a book and seemed unbothered by my attention. I kept thinking about the hours required to create those paintings, the precision necessary for a canvas perhaps a quarter-inch wide, the question of why someone would make something so beautiful and so temporary—because nails grow out, and then the paintings are gone forever.

I never saw that woman again. She was probably a complete stranger I'll never have another interaction with. But the image of her hands has stuck with me. It's strange what we retain. I couldn't tell you what most of the people I see look like, but I can see those tiny painted mountains perfectly.

Maybe this is what art does, or what any deliberate making does—it creates something that catches the attention sideways, that makes people notice things they weren't looking for. A book, a song, a small painting on a fingernail. It's a way of saying: look here, notice this, this particular configuration of things is worth your attention.

I think we're all starved for this. We're all walking through a world we're not actually seeing, and we're all aching to be noticed in return, to have our own particular configurations of being seen and recognized and taken as genuine. We want our tiny painted mountains to matter to someone.

This might be why I love noticing things so much. It's a form of care, even when it's directed at something inanimate. To really see a thing—the particular way shadows fall across a particular building, the specific configuration of moss on a particular stone—is to honor it with attention. It's to say: you exist, and you are worth seeing.

The world is composed of infinite such things, each one specific and unrepeatable and ultimately unknown by almost everyone. And somehow that's okay. It's okay that my painted mountains moment with the subway woman will mean nothing to the vast machinery of the universe. It's okay that most of the interesting things I notice will be noticed by no one but me. The noticing itself is the point.

Maybe this is all I'm really trying to do with any kind of thought or writing—to notice something, to slow down enough to actually perceive rather than just pass through, and then to share that noticing, even if no one else will ever care. The small act of witness. The insistence that this particular thing, this specific arrangement of circumstances or light or human gesture, was here and it mattered.

That's enough. That has to be enough.
